import { Steps, Aside, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import SeqDiagram from '../../../components/SeqDiagram.astro';
import BuildAppPipeline from '../../../components/diagrams/BuildAppPipeline.astro';

This tutorial walks one path from nothing to a running key-value app on the
component SDK (`calimero-sdk`): you write a small Rust crate, test it on the
real engine, build it into a `calimero:app` component, create a context (an app
instance) from it on a local cluster, call its methods, and share it with a
second person, checking the output at each step.

The app is a smaller cousin of core's [`apps/kv-store`](/build/examples/#start-here):
where that one keeps an `UnorderedMap`, this one keeps a `Table` of records and
a `Counter`, the two state types most apps start from.

<BuildAppPipeline />

<Aside type="note">
  The code on this page is complete: the crate, its test and its scenario
  build and pass as shown against `calimero-sdk` at 1.0.0-rc.20. The commands
  are `crates/merod` and the CLI definitions in
  `crates/meroctl/src`; every command is in the
  [meroctl reference](/operate/meroctl/).
</Aside>

## 1. Prerequisites

<Steps>

1. **Rust with the `wasm32-wasip2` target**, and a checkout of
   [core](https://github.com/calimero-network/core) for the node and the
   tools:

   ```sh
   rustup target add wasm32-wasip2
   git clone https://github.com/calimero-network/core && cd core
   cargo install --locked --path crates/meroctl
   cargo install --locked --path crates/merod
   ```

2. **A development cluster.** `meroctl local up` starts `merod local` in the
   background: three nodes in one process on `127.0.0.1:2501`-`2503`, with
   mock attestation. It saves the first node in `meroctl` as `local`:

   ```sh
   meroctl local up
   ```

   `meroctl local down` stops it.

3. **Sign in.** Sign up with a passkey kept in a file (development clusters
   only):

   ```sh
   meroctl login --dev-passkey ./dev-passkey.json --name alice
   ```

   `login` signs up when the file does not exist yet and saves the session.
   The sign-up also makes alice's personal organization, where her contexts
   go unless she names another. See
   [Run local nodes](/contribute/development/#run-local-nodes).

</Steps>

## 2. Create the project

An app is a standalone `cdylib` crate that depends on the SDK and nothing else
from Calimero. `calimero-sdk` is not on crates.io: take it from core's git
repository at the release your cluster runs.

```text
kv-store/
├── Cargo.toml
├── src/lib.rs
├── tests/app.rs
└── scenarios/basic.json
```

`Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[package]
name = "kv-store"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib"]

[dependencies]
calimero-sdk = { git = "https://github.com/calimero-network/core", tag = "1.0.0-rc.20" }

# The test harness (TestApp) and the builder, for `cargo test` on the host.
[target.'cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))'.dev-dependencies]
calimero-sdk = { git = "https://github.com/calimero-network/core", tag = "1.0.0-rc.20", features = ["testing"] }
calimero-app-build = { git = "https://github.com/calimero-network/core", tag = "1.0.0-rc.20" }
serde_json = "1"

# Its own workspace root.
[workspace]
```

## 3. Define the state

State is a struct of handles annotated with `#[app::state]`. Loading it reads
nothing: each field names its own range of keys in the app's storage, after
the field's camelCase name. Records live in a `Table`, declared with
`#[derive(Record)]` and a `#[table]` attribute naming the key (and any indexes,
unique constraints and counts, see [Tables & Collections](/build/collections/)).

Start `src/lib.rs`:

```rust
//! A string key-value store shared by the members of the app's organization.

use calimero_sdk::prelude::*;

/// One stored value, keyed by `key`.
#[derive(Record)]
#[table(key = "key")]
pub struct Entry {
    pub key: String,
    pub value: String,
}

/// The app's state: a table of entries and how many there are.
#[app::state(version = 1)]
pub struct KvStore {
    entries: Table<Entry>,
    size: Counter,
}
```

The app runs on its cluster's leader, which orders every write in the app's
log, so a later `set` of a key replaces an earlier one: there is nothing to
merge. `Counter::add` is an add the host applies without a read, so `size`
stays exact under any number of writers.

## 4. Add logic, events and errors

Add the logic block, the events and the errors to the same file. Every app has
one `#[app::init]`; a `&mut self` method is a call (a write the leader logs),
a `#[app::view]` reads:

```rust
#[app::logic]
impl KvStore {
    /// Runs once, as the owner, when the app is created.
    #[app::init]
    pub fn init() -> app::Result<Self> {
        Ok(Self::load())
    }

    /// Stores `value` under `key`, replacing any value already there.
    pub fn set(&mut self, key: String, value: String) -> app::Result<()> {
        let event = if self.entries.contains(&key)? {
            Event::Updated { key: key.clone(), value: value.clone() }
        } else {
            self.size.add(1)?;
            Event::Inserted { key: key.clone(), value: value.clone() }
        };
        self.entries.upsert(Entry { key, value })?;
        env::emit(event, Audience::All)?;
        Ok(())
    }

    /// Removes `key`; says whether it was there.
    pub fn remove(&mut self, key: String) -> app::Result<bool> {
        if !self.entries.remove(&key)? {
            return Ok(false);
        }
        self.size.add(-1)?;
        env::emit(Event::Removed { key }, Audience::All)?;
        Ok(true)
    }

    /// The value under `key`, or `null`.
    #[app::view]
    pub fn get(&self, key: String) -> app::Result<Option<String>> {
        Ok(self.entries.get(&key)?.map(|e| e.value))
    }

    /// The value under `key`, or the app error `NotFound`.
    #[app::view]
    pub fn get_result(&self, key: String) -> app::Result<String> {
        match self.entries.get(&key)? {
            Some(e) => Ok(e.value),
            None => Err(Error::NotFound { key }.into()),
        }
    }

    /// How many keys are stored (a `u64`: a decimal string on the wire).
    #[app::view]
    pub fn len(&self) -> app::Result<u64> {
        Ok(self.size.get()?)
    }
}

/// A change to the store, emitted after the write that caused it.
#[app::event]
pub enum Event {
    Inserted { key: String, value: String },
    Updated { key: String, value: String },
    Removed { key: String },
}

/// A typed failure: `{ code, fields }` on the wire.
#[app::error]
pub enum Error {
    NotFound { key: String },
}
```

A few things to notice:

- Method and argument names reach the ABI in camelCase: `get_result` is
  `getResult`.
- `#[app::event]` and `#[app::error]` must be in the same module as
  `#[app::logic]`, where the ABI picks them up; every field has a name.
- `env::emit` sends an `#[app::event]` value to an audience (`All`, the caller,
  named accounts, a team, the organization or its admins). It is delivered only
  if the call succeeds.
- An `#[app::error]` variant reaches the client as `422 APP_ERROR` with
  `{ "code": "NotFound", "fields": { "key": ".." } }`. A failed call writes
  nothing and emits nothing.
- `u64` and `i64` arguments and results travel as decimal strings, so `len`
  answers `"1"`, not `1`.
- `?` works on every SDK call: storage and table errors convert into
  `AppError`.

## 5. Test it

`calimero_sdk::testing::TestApp` runs the built component on the real
wasmtime engine, in an organization you describe, as named accounts, with the
node's own checks. `tests/app.rs`:

```rust
#![cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))]

use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};

use calimero_app_build::build_component;
use calimero_sdk::testing::{run_scenario, Failure, Org, TestApp};
use serde_json::json;

/// This crate built as a `calimero:app` component.
fn component() -> Vec<u8> {
    let dir = Path::new(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"));
    let target = PathBuf::from(env!("CARGO_TARGET_TMPDIR")).join("guest");
    build_component(dir, &target).expect("build the component").component
}

#[test]
fn set_get_remove() {
    let mut t = TestApp::new(&component(), Org::new().members(["bob"]), 1_700_000_000_000);

    t.as_("bob").call("set", json!({ "key": "k", "value": "v" })).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(t.as_("owner").view("get", json!({ "key": "k" })).unwrap(), json!("v"));
    assert_eq!(t.as_("owner").view("len", json!({})).unwrap(), json!("1"));
    assert_eq!(t.events_for("owner")[0].0, "Inserted");

    match t.as_("owner").view("getResult", json!({ "key": "x" })) {
        Err(Failure::App { code, fields }) => {
            assert_eq!(code, "NotFound");
            assert_eq!(fields, json!({ "key": "x" }));
        }
        other => panic!("expected NotFound, got {other:?}"),
    }

    assert_eq!(t.as_("bob").call("remove", json!({ "key": "k" })).unwrap(), json!(true));
    assert_eq!(t.as_("owner").view("len", json!({})).unwrap(), json!("0"));
}

#[test]
fn scenario() {
    let dir = Path::new(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"));
    let mut t = TestApp::new(&component(), Org::new().members(["bob"]), 1_700_000_000_000);
    run_scenario(&mut t, &dir.join("scenarios/basic.json")).unwrap();
}
```

`TestApp::new` runs `init` as the account `"owner"`; `Org::new().members(..)`
adds the other accounts the app's organization holds. The same steps can live
in a scenario file, which `run_scenario` runs here and the node's cluster
runner can run on real nodes ([Testing](/build/testing/)).
`scenarios/basic.json`:

```json
[
  { "as": "bob", "op": "call", "method": "set", "args": { "key": "k", "value": "v" },
    "events": { "owner": ["Inserted"] } },
  { "as": "owner", "op": "view", "method": "get", "args": { "key": "k" }, "expect": { "ok": "v" } },
  { "as": "owner", "op": "view", "method": "len", "args": {}, "expect": { "ok": "1" } },
  { "as": "owner", "op": "view", "method": "getResult", "args": { "key": "x" },
    "expect": { "error": "NotFound", "fields": { "key": "x" } } }
]
```

Run both:

```sh
cargo test
```

```text
running 2 tests
test scenario ... ok
test set_get_remove ... ok

test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
```

The first run builds the component for `wasm32-wasip2` and compiles wasmtime,
so it takes a while; later runs reuse both.

## 6. Build and run

Build the component:

```sh
meroctl app build path/to/kv-store --out kv_store.wasm
```

It compiles the crate for `wasm32-wasip2`, wraps it as a `calimero:app`
component and lifts the ABI into the component's `calimero:abi` section, which
the node reads to dispatch and gate calls ([App interface](/build/app-abi/)).

<Steps>

1. **Create a context** from it. On a development cluster `--path` uploads a
   raw `.wasm` (a real cluster installs signed `.mpk` packages, see
   [Packaging & signing](/build/packaging-signing/)); `init` runs as you:

   ```sh
   meroctl context create --name my-kv --path kv_store.wasm --alias my-kv
   ```

2. **Call the setter.** A call without `--view` is a write the leader logs:

   ```sh
   meroctl call -c my-kv set --args '{"key": "hello", "value": "world"}'
   ```

3. **Read it back** with a view:

   ```sh
   meroctl call -c my-kv get --args '{"key": "hello"}' --view
   ```

   ```json
   { "index": <n>, "result": "world", "receipt": { … } }
   ```

   `index` is the log index of the state the view read; the receipt is signed
   by the node that answered.

4. **Follow its events** (stop with Ctrl-C, or `--limit N`):

   ```sh
   meroctl context watch my-kv --from 0
   ```

</Steps>

## 7. Make it multi-user

A context belongs to an organization, and the organization decides who reaches
it. Create one, create the context in it, and invite a second person:

<Steps>

1. **Create an organization** and a context in it. `namespace create` answers
   the new organization's id as `orgId`:

   ```sh
   meroctl namespace create acme
   meroctl context create --name team-kv --path kv_store.wasm \
     --namespace <org-id> --alias team-kv
   ```

   A context created in an organization is reached by every member (access
   `org`, the default there).

2. **Invite** a member. An invite is approved with your passkey, so pass the
   file on a development cluster; the answer carries the invitation `token`:

   ```sh
   meroctl namespace invite <org-id> --role member --dev-passkey ./dev-passkey.json
   ```

3. **Join** as the second person: a second account, with its own passkey file,
   on the same cluster. Save the node under another `--home` so the two
   sessions stay apart:

   ```sh
   meroctl --home ./bob node add local http://127.0.0.1:2501/ --allow-mock
   meroctl --home ./bob login --dev-passkey ./bob-passkey.json --name bob
   meroctl --home ./bob namespace join <token>
   ```

4. **Write as one, read as the other**. Aliases are per account, so bob names
   the context by its id (`meroctl context get team-kv` shows it):

   ```sh
   meroctl --home ./bob call -c <context-id> set --args '{"key": "from", "value": "bob"}'
   meroctl call -c team-kv get --args '{"key": "from"}' --view
   ```

   ```json
   { "index": <n>, "result": "bob", "receipt": { … } }
   ```

</Steps>

Both people wrote and read the same state, each with their own passkey,
through any node of the cluster. The organization decides who reaches the
context; what each member may change inside it is the app's own code and its
[access control](/build/guides/access-control/). See
[Organizations, teams & access](/protocol/organizations/).
